children: Three AI-era giants have amassed valuations that tower over the combined first-day value of thousands of U.S. tech companies that went public over the past 45 years.

were valued at a combined $5.2T, compared with $4.1T for 3,365 U.S. technology IPOs between 1980 and 2025, according to a chart shared by Jason on X. The three-company figure comprised $2T for SpaceX, $2T for Anthropic, and $1.2T for OpenAI.

The comparison captured how dramatically the center of gravity in technology had shifted toward a small group of private companies building AI, space, and related infrastructure. OpenAI and Anthropic alone accounted for about $3.2T, or roughly 62%, of the combined valuation shown in the chart, even though neither had yet reached the public markets.

SpaceX provided the public-market reality check. The company priced its June IPO at $135 a share, valuing the company at about $1.75T, and its shares opened at $150 before closing their first trading session at $160.95. The debut close put SpaceX's market value at roughly $2.1T, while the company had raised about $75B in the IPO.

SpaceX shares subsequently climbed as high as $225.64, marking the stock's record intraday high, before giving back much of those gains. The shares closed Monday at $151.85, leaving them about 5.7% below their first-day close and roughly 32.7% below the record high.

OpenAI, meanwhile, has delayed plans for an IPO and was not expected to go public in 2026. CEO Sam Altman had cited AI safety concerns around the timing of a listing, while the company has been linked to a valuation of around $1T or more in private-market discussions.

Anthropic has also been weighing a public listing, with reports pointing to a potential November IPO. The company has reportedly been considering a valuation of as much as $2T, although the timing and terms remain subject to change.

The AI angle made the comparison particularly striking. The valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic reflected investor expectations around the commercial potential of frontier AI, while SpaceX represented a broader technology story spanning satellites, connectivity, and increasingly AI-related infrastructure.

The three companies therefore offered a snapshot of how enormous pools of capital were being directed toward a handful of technology platforms while the AI industry was demanding massive investment in computing and infrastructure.

title: Three AI-era giants tower over 45 years of tech IPOs
